content: Astronomers have discovered a star slowly eating its companion in an extraordinary cosmic feast that could last billions of years. A small star about 300 light-years from Earth is feeding on a companion that circles it every 87 minutes. The two objects are remarkably close, yet the star is drawing away material slowly enough that the feeding could continue for hundreds of thousands or even billions of years. The pair, named ZTF J0440+2325, lies within the Milky Way. Its smaller member is a brown dwarf, a planetlike object that falls between planets and stars in mass. The brown dwarf has about 25 times Jupiter’s mass, while the star has about 85 times Jupiter’s mass. Both are small by stellar standards, and the brown dwarf’s entire orbit could fit within the Sun’s diameter. Most planets occupy stable orbits that keep them apart from their stars. Astronomers have observed plenty of these systems, along with a handful of stars rapidly engulfing planets that come too close. The new discovery reveals another possibility. Reported by scientists at MIT and other institutions in an October 5, 2026, paper in Nature Astronomy , it represents the first observation of a low-mass star slowly and steadily consuming material from another low-mass object. Several years ago, Kevin Burdge, an assistant professor of physics at MIT, noticed an unusual brightness pattern while reviewing data from the Zwicky Transient Facility, or ZTF. The facility uses a camera on a telescope at California’s Palomar Observatory to scan for rapid brightness changes that could signal a supernova, a gamma-ray burst, or colliding neutron stars. A supernova’s light curve, a record of brightness over time, resembles a bell as the exploding star brightens and then fades. The light curve that caught Burdge’s attention instead showed a repeating triangular pattern. “I remember first looking at this and thinking, stars don’t make triangular waveforms like this,” he recalls. At the time, Burdge and his colleagues were investigating a different signal, which they identified as a “black widow binary.” In that kind of system, an extremely dense, spinning neutron star slowly consumes a much smaller companion star, behavior that evokes its spider namesake. Burdge wondered whether the triangular signal came from another black widow. In those systems, however, the light shows a pronounced wobble as the lightweight companion whips around the much heavier neutron star. “We weren’t seeing that whipping back and forth here,” Burdge says. “It didn’t make any sense. We couldn’t explain what this was.” Recently, Burdge returned to the unexplained signal with Aaron Householder, a graduate student in MIT’s Department of Earth, Atmospheric, and Planetary Sciences. They wanted to test an idea Burdge and his colleagues had considered years earlier. “If you have less mass in the system overall, things can gently orbit each other without whipping back and forth,” Burdge says. “That was the idea. But we never had any proof. And this weird triangle just sat for years.” Using the original ZTF signal to locate the source, the researchers directed multiple telescopes toward it. They measured several properties, including a small but detectable wobble, and compared the motion with that of black widows and similar binary systems. “That was the real clincher for this system,” Householder says. “When we measured that wobble, we found we were not seeing a black widow. This was a low-mass star that’s orbited by a brown dwarf. The wobble was too small in amplitude to be anything else.” With the objects’ masses and tight orbit established, the team investigated whether one could be pulling material from the other. This process, called accretion, is most often observed around compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars, which pack enormous mass into a small space. When a black hole draws matter from a much smaller nearby object, the material gathers around it in a disk. “The difference here is, the thing absorbing matter is not a tiny black hole but a star, which is relatively big in size,” Burdge explains. “So matter just pummels directly onto the surface, at very high speeds, like an asteroid hitting the moon.” The researchers tested that possibility with simulations based on the properties of the star and brown dwarf. They modeled particles of matter on the brown dwarf and used the laws of physics and equations of motion to track where those particles would travel over time. “When we track those test particles, we see they indeed fall right onto the surface of the star,” Householder says. “This is the first time we’ve caught a low-mass star actively accreting from another low-mass object.” The team then considered how the steady stream would appear from a distance as the brown dwarf and its flowing material circled the star. “It’s like you’ve got this continuous fireball onto one of the objects, and as one orbits the other, that hotspot comes in and out of view, and the peak of the triangle signal is when you’re looking right at the fireball,” Burdge explains. The researchers calculated that the brown dwarf must be supplying about 1/100,000 of Earth’s mass in material each year. To convey the scale, they compared the flow to about 40 million dump trucks’ worth of material, or roughly 1.3 trillion one-pound burritos every second. Even that enormous quantity represents only a small fraction of the brown dwarf’s mass, making the estimated transfer slow and steady relative to the available supply. “When we think of stars interacting with planets or brown dwarfs, the picture is always that the star eventually swallows the other thing,” says Burdge. “This is what will happen to the Earth when the Sun becomes a red giant. But here, we’ve found an alternative: Instead of swallowing the thing up, the star can gradually eat it, for billions of years.” Alongside Burdge and Householder, the study’s MIT coauthors include Kaitlyn Shin, Saul Rappaport, Joheen Chakraborty, and Emma Chickles. The collaboration also includes researchers from Caltech, the University of Hawaii, the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias and the Universidad de La Laguna in Spain, and the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. With an explanation for the triangular light curve, the team hopes to identify other nearby systems where stars gradually draw material from their companions. “It’s inspiring a lot of new searches on our part,” Householder says. “I think we’re going to learn a lot about a different kind of way that planets and brown dwarfs interact with their host stars.” Reference: “Stable mass transfer from a substellar object onto an M dwarf” by Aaron Householder, Kaitlyn Shin, Kevin B. Burdge, Thomas R. Marsh, Saul A. Rappaport, Kareem El-Badry, Joheen Chakraborty, Emma Chickles, Fei Dai, Matthew J. Graham, S. R. Kulkarni, Pablo Rodríguez-Gil, Andrew Vanderburg and Samuel Whitebook, 5 October 2026, Nature Astronomy . DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02992-6 This research was supported, in part, by the National Science Foundation. Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. title: Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
content: Astronomers analyzing white dwarf stars have for the first time found a star that would appear green to human eyes, according to a new study. While for most stars, color is temperature-dependent and limited to a few hues, white dwarfs, which are the dense remnants of sun-like stars that have died, can glow in an incredible range of colors, said lead study author Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick, England, on Thursday. “The colors that normal stars can have are pretty much only orange, white or blue,” Hollands told CNN. “What we found is, for most white dwarfs, that’s the same as well. But there are some special cases where the physics in the outer layers of these stars are sufficiently strange that it causes actually quite big deviations in terms of their spectrum,” he said. These deviations are due to the interaction between the helium in their atmosphere and traces of other elements, which vary between white dwarfs, depending on what material has interacted with the star over the course of its lifetime. For instance, iron, magnesium and sodium, elements commonly found in rocks, can be found on the surface — potential evidence of a nearby former planetary system, or from “something like an asteroid that ventures too close to the white dwarf,” Hollands explained. “It gets shredded up into dust, and then those rocky bits of dust and debris fall onto the white dwarf,” he said. “And then that gets mixed into the outer layers, and then you can actually use that to measure what the rocky stuff was made off,” said Hollands. “So we can actually use the white dwarf as a sort of diagnostic tool to actually measure the chemistry of planetary material,” he added. “The white dwarf is taking apart the planets, and we’re able to see what was actually inside that planet — the proportion of the different elements — and that gives us clues in how these planets were formed,” said Adam Burgasser, a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of California San Diego. “It is a crime scene, and we’re kind of piecing through the evidence that we have left available to us, and that’s allowing us to kind of piece the story of what the planet was and how it was made way, way, way back in in history.” For this study, Hollands looked at the 151 known white dwarf stars that are within 20 parsecs, or around 65 light years, of Earth. As for the green star, the main elements present are calcium, sodium and lithium, Hollands said. “It kind of stimulated interest in me in looking more at that object and why it has so much material being accreted onto it,” said Burgasser, who was not involved in the study. “It can it can excite the public as well as the scientists in learning more about some of the more, I would say, extreme objects in this sample.” Another notable star was “almost like a salmon pink,” due to the presence of a high density of carbon molecules, Hollands added. While no white dwarf stars can be seen directly from Earth, Hollands was able to calculate their color using star spectrum data, which a statement from the researchers defines as “the ‘fingerprint’ produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, much like a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow.” Hollands explained that the research has also brought these space objects much closer to home. “It gives you a nice human connection to these very distant things that are so far away that sometimes even as a researcher you feel quite disconnected from these objects that you study,” he said. “But then you can sort of add a human element into it and it feels a lot more tangible.” The observations about green star are based on existing data and may not shed new understandings about white dwarfs, but the study does offer an intriguing approach and view of these celestial bodies, said Agnès Kim, an astrophysicist and professor of physics at Penn State Scranton, who was not involved in the work. “Doing a study that goes from spectrum to what the human eye would see is a cool intersection of physics and biology to me,” Kim wrote in an email. “I love that some would look green to us if they were close enough for us to see them, and even more fun that some would look pink.” Burgasser added that the study’s categorization scheme using temperatures and atmospheric properties can be useful for the field moving forward. “Some things are kind of purplish pink, and some other things were greenish and blue — and that kind of classification, which by the way we do all the time in astronomy, is classify things, allows us to focus on: why are these types of objects these colors, and are they related to each other based on their composition?” Burgasser said. “We have that information in other forms, but I think this is maybe a simplified way of organizing that data.” Next, Hollands is planning to keep analyzing more white dwarf star spectra, with advances in scientific techniques meaning that researchers will be able to look at a new tranche of stars that are even farther away from Earth. “We know of white dwarfs that we don’t have spectra for,” he said, “but that’s all about to change because there’s quite a few spectroscopic surveys” that are going to start delivering data. “We’ll be getting a tenfold increase in the number of white dwarfs that have spectra,” Hollands said. “And so maybe if we’re lucky, we’ll go from one or maybe two green white dwarfs to 10 or 20.” The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, or RASTI.

Nature may have fewer backup plans than we thought, leaving our food supply and climate more exposed when species disappear. The largest global study of its kind suggests that losing species can steadily erode the benefits ecosystems provide, including pollination, clean water, carbon storage, and natural pest control. Led by King’s College London and Imperial College London , the research challenges the assumption that many species are interchangeable and that a few losses make little difference. Working with the Natural History Museum and the Alan Turing Institute, the researchers combined 423 published studies and 222,829 data points from land, freshwater, marine, and estuarine ecosystems. Published in Nature Ecology & Evolution , their analysis produced a database more than twice the size of the largest previous effort. Across 23 categories of ecosystem services and functions, most benefits kept increasing as biodiversity rose. They generally did not level off once a small collection of species was present, suggesting that ecosystems have less spare capacity than scientists previously assumed. The findings call into question the extent of “functional redundancy,” the idea that different species can perform similar jobs and compensate when one disappears. If that backup were widespread, additional species would eventually contribute little to a particular service. Instead, the study found that greater diversity usually continued to bring benefits. Dr. Emma Moffett, the study’s lead author and a geography lecturer at King’s College London, said, “Our findings challenge the comfortable assumption has been that ecosystems carry plenty of backup, so losing a species here and there doesn’t change much. Across most of the benefits ecosystems provide that we looked at, the data doesn’t support that. The ecological benefits keep climbing as diversity rises, which means it is falling as we lose species.” There were exceptions. Protection against coastal flooding, erosion, and similar hazards showed relatively little sensitivity to biodiversity overall. These functions often depend heavily on a few foundational species, such as shrubs whose roots stabilize sand dunes. Conservation needs to account for both overall biodiversity and the outsized contributions of certain species. Protecting a wide range of species helps sustain many ecosystem benefits, while safeguarding foundational species preserves functions that others may be unable to replace. The strongest relationship between biodiversity and any measured service involved marine carbon sequestration, the capture and storage of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) in ocean waters and sediments. This suggests that species losses could have especially important consequences for the ocean’s contribution to climate protection. Marine life helps move carbon through the ocean, from phytoplankton near the surface to microbial food webs involved in transferring it into deeper water. The findings point to the importance of diverse communities for blue carbon sinks in the ocean and coastal environments, including mangroves and salt marshes. However, the striking ocean result came from only a small number of datasets. The researchers identify this shortage of evidence as an urgent research gap, so the finding warrants further investigation. Dr. Moffett said, “The ocean result stopped us in our tracks. Carbon capture at sea responded to biodiversity more strongly than anything else we measured, and yet it’s one of the least studied areas we found. If the world is counting on blue carbon to help with climate change, marine life can’t be an afterthought.” The team also explored how these benefits could change by connecting its database to biodiversity projections under the socioeconomic scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. One focus was natural pest control on farmland, where predators and other enemies of crop pests provide a service farmers receive for free. The model predicts that this protection would weaken under development driven by fossil fuels compared with a pathway less dependent on them. Countries experiencing rapid population growth and lower levels of development would face the sharpest losses. Dr. Will Pearse, an associate professor in evolutionary ecology in Imperial College London’s Department of Life Sciences, said, “We’ve known that biodiversity supports humanity by providing us with food, clean water, clean air, and so many other ecosystem services. But what this model gives us is a precise, global picture: we can now predict the benefits biodiversity provides anywhere, making it even easier to recognize and take advantage of those benefits.” The database and forecasts for all 23 categories are publicly available to support policy and planning. Reference: “Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide” by Emma R. Moffett, Joel H. Gayford, Lexi Chen, Olivia F. Morris, Yuming Shi, Lucy Somekh, Nicole Stasik, Andy Purvis, Guy Woodward and William D. Pearse, 6 October 2026, Nature Ecology & Evolution .
